clinicalPearls: A descriptive term for severe hyperkeratotic disorders producing thick, spiny, verrucous scale that resembles porcupine quills
The Curth-Macklin type is an autosomal dominant condition caused by variants in KRT1 (keratin 1)
Unlike epidermolytic ichthyosis, the Curth-Macklin form typically lacks widespread blistering despite prominent hyperkeratosis
Lesions may be generalised or arranged in a linear or systematised naevoid pattern following the lines of Blaschko when the disorder is mosaic
A severe palmoplantar keratoderma is frequently present and can cause functional impairment
Diagnosis is clinical and histological; electron microscopy classically shows perinuclear shells of keratin filaments, and molecular testing can identify the KRT1 variant
Management is supportive with intensive emollients and keratolytics, and oral retinoids may reduce the burden of hyperkeratosis in severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Ichthyosis hystrix of the Curth-Macklin type is caused by variants in KRT1, which encodes keratin 1, a component of the suprabasal keratin intermediate filament network. The variants disrupt normal filament assembly, producing aggregated perinuclear keratin shells and abnormal terminal differentiation of keratinocytes. This leads to gross retention hyperkeratosis with the characteristic spiny, verrucous scale, while the specific filament defect accounts for the relative absence of the fragility and blistering seen in classical epidermolytic ichthyosis from other keratin variants.
additionalDifferentials: Epidermal naevus and systematised epidermolytic naevus
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing marked hyperkeratosis and abnormal keratinocyte differentiation
Electron microscopy for perinuclear keratin shells (Curth-Macklin type)
Molecular genetic testing of KRT1 and related keratin genes
Assessment of palmoplantar involvement and function
Screening for secondary infection of fissured hyperkeratosis
redFlags: Extensive barrier failure with recurrent infection and fluid or temperature dysregulation
Disabling palmoplantar keratoderma with deep painful fissures
Rapid change in an established lesion suggesting alternative pathology
Signs of secondary cutaneous or systemic infection
reference.prognosis: The disorder is lifelong and can be physically and cosmetically disabling, but with sustained emollient and keratolytic care, and retinoids where appropriate, many patients achieve worthwhile reduction in scale.
pitfalls: Assuming all severe keratin-related ichthyoses blister and overlooking the non-blistering Curth-Macklin type
Not recognising a systematised naevoid variant as a mosaic form of the disorder
Underusing emollients and keratolytics before considering systemic therapy
management: Reduce the thick spiny scale with sustained emollient and keratolytic therapy (urea, lactic acid, salicylic acid) as the mainstay
Offer systemic retinoids for severe disease under specialist supervision, weighing modest benefit against side effects
Manage severe palmoplantar keratoderma with keratolytics, regular paring or debridement and podiatry to preserve function
Screen for and treat secondary infection of fissured hyperkeratosis
Confirm the diagnosis by histology and electron microscopy (perinuclear keratin shells) with KRT1 testing
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, including mosaic Blaschko-distributed disease, within dermatology and clinical genetics
